title: La entrevista médica: Interviewing in Spanish
summary: Conduct a structured medical interview in Spanish, using past tenses to build a patient's story.

lessons.title: Chief Complaint and Present Illness: Preterite vs. Imperfect

levels.kid:
When you feel sick, the doctor asks, **"¿Qué le pasa?"** That means "What's wrong?"

You might answer:
- **Me duele la panza.** (My tummy hurts.)
- **Me duele la cabeza.** (My head hurts.)

Then the doctor wants the story. Stories happen in the past, and Spanish has two past "helpers."

One helper is for things that happened once, like a door slamming: **Me caí.** (I fell.)

The other helper paints the background, like the scenery in a movie: **Estaba jugando.** (I was playing.)

Put them together: **Estaba jugando y me caí.** (I was playing and I fell.)

When did it start? **Ayer** means yesterday. Now the doctor knows your story!
levels.hs:
Every medical interview starts with the **motivo de consulta** (chief complaint), the main reason the patient came in. Common opening questions use the polite **usted** form:
- **¿Qué le trae por aquí hoy?** (What brings you here today?)
- **¿En qué le puedo ayudar?** (How can I help you?)

Next comes the **enfermedad actual** (history of present illness, HPI), the story of the problem. In Mexico you will also hear **padecimiento actual**. Because this story is in the past, you need two past tenses.

The **preterite (pretérito)** reports completed events with a clear start or end:
- **Empezó el lunes.** (It started on Monday.)
- **Vomité dos veces.** (I vomited twice.)

The **imperfect (imperfecto)** describes background, ongoing states, or habits in the past:
- **Me dolía mucho.** (It was hurting a lot.)
- **Estaba en el trabajo.** (I was at work.)

A real example. A patient with a headache says: **"Estaba en el trabajo cuando me empezó un dolor muy fuerte."** (I was at work when a very strong pain started.) The imperfect sets the scene and the preterite marks the event.

To ask how long something has lasted, use **hace + time + que**: **"Hace tres días que me duele"** means the pain started three days ago and is still going. You can also ask **¿Desde cuándo?** (Since when?).
levels.college:
The HPI is a timeline, and Spanish encodes timeline structure in its tense choice. Mastering this lets you both ask precise questions and understand the patient's answers.

**Preterite: events on the timeline.** Single actions, sequences, and bounded episodes. Signal words include **ayer, anoche, de repente, el martes, hace dos horas**.
- **Me desmayé.** (I fainted.)
- **Fui a urgencias.** (I went to the ER.) *Fue, fui, tuve, estuve, vino* are high-yield irregulars.

**Imperfect: the background.** Ongoing states, descriptions, and repeated or habitual actions. Signal words include **mientras, todos los días, siempre, a veces, cuando era niño**.
- **Tenía fiebre.** (I had a fever, an ongoing state.)
- **Me dolía todas las noches.** (It hurt every night.)

**The interrupted-action frame:** imperfect (often progressive) + **cuando** + preterite. **Estaba caminando cuando sentí el dolor.** This is ideal for onset questions: **¿Qué estaba haciendo cuando empezó?**

**Characterizing the symptom in Spanish (OPQRST-style):**
- Onset: **¿Cuándo empezó? ¿Empezó de repente o poco a poco?**
- Provocation: **¿Qué lo mejora? ¿Qué lo empeora?**
- Quality: **¿Cómo es el dolor? ¿Punzante, opresivo, quemante?**
- Radiation: **¿Dónde le duele? ¿Se le corre a otra parte?**
- Severity: **Del uno al diez, ¿qué tan fuerte es?**
- Timing: **¿Es constante o va y viene?**

**Duration constructions:** **Hace + time + que + present** describes something still ongoing (**Hace una semana que tengo tos**). **Hace + time** with the preterite marks a point in the past (**Empezó hace una semana**).

Close the HPI by summarizing back in the third person: **Entonces, el dolor empezó ayer de repente y desde entonces es constante.**
levels.phd:
Aspect, not time, is the core distinction. Both tenses refer to the past; the **preterite** is **perfective** (it views the event as a bounded whole), while the **imperfect** is **imperfective** (it views the situation from inside, without its endpoints). This is why the same verb can carry different clinical meanings:
- **Estuve mareado toda la mañana.** A bounded episode, now resolved.
- **Estaba mareado cuando me levanté.** A state in progress at a reference point, with no claim that it ended.

For symptom chronology, that difference matters. A preterite implies resolution unless the patient adds otherwise, so follow up with **¿Todavía lo tiene?** (Do you still have it?).

**Lexical meaning shifts in the preterite** occur with stative verbs:
- **Supe que tenía diabetes en 2019.** (I found out...) vs. **Sabía** (I knew).
- **Tuve una convulsión.** (I had a seizure, an event) vs. **tenía dolor** (I had pain, a state).
- **Pude caminar** (I managed to walk) vs. **podía caminar** (I was able to walk, in general).

**Reported speech** backshifts into the imperfect: **El médico me dijo que tenía una infección.** Patients often relay prior diagnoses this way, so read the imperfect as "the doctor said I had," not as an ongoing habit.

**Pluperfect for sequence:** **Cuando llegó la ambulancia, ya me había despertado.** (When the ambulance arrived, I had already woken up.) This preserves order in loss-of-consciousness histories.

**Dialectal variation:** In much of Spain the **pretérito perfecto** (*he vomitado*) is used for completed events within the current time frame ("today"), where most Latin American speakers use the preterite (*vomité*). Both mean the event is finished. Don't read the present perfect as ongoing.

**The accidental "se"** frames symptoms as happening to the patient: **Se me durmió el brazo** (My arm went numb), **Se me olvidó** (I forgot). These are highly natural in HPIs and worth recognizing.
levels.expert:
Clinically, tense errors create false timelines. Practical pitfalls and refinements:

- **Don't over-rely on yes/no questions.** Patients often agree to be polite. Open prompts like **Cuénteme qué pasó** (Tell me what happened) and **¿Y luego?** (And then?) generate a narrative you can map onto tenses.
- **Anchor dates to events, not calendars.** **¿Empezó antes o después de la cena?** often gives better precision than "what time."
- **Clarify "de repente."** Patients use it loosely. For a possible thunderclap headache, ask **¿El dolor llegó a su máximo en segundos o en minutos?** and **¿Es el peor dolor de cabeza de su vida?** Pair this with an interrupted-action frame: **¿Qué estaba haciendo exactamente cuando le empezó?**
- **Seizure and syncope histories** need a witness and a strict sequence: **¿Qué recuerda antes? ¿Alguien lo vio? ¿Cuánto tiempo duró? ¿Se mordió la lengua? ¿Estaba confundido después?** The preterite marks discrete events; the imperfect captures the post-event state.
- **Watch out for "ayer" vs "anoche."** Some patients count a night-time symptom as "hoy" (today) once it passes midnight. Restate the timeline to confirm it.
- **Distinguish recurrence from a new symptom.** **¿Le ha pasado esto antes?** opens the topic. An imperfect answer (**me pasaba de niño**) suggests a pattern; a preterite answer (**me pasó una vez**) suggests a single prior episode.
- **Use usted for adults by default.** Switch to tú only if the patient invites it or is a child.

**Summarize with a teach-back of the timeline.** Repeating the story back, for example **A ver si entendí: estaba trabajando, de repente le dio el dolor, vomitó una vez y sigue con dolor, ¿correcto?**, catches aspect misreadings before they reach the chart.

**Open question for learners:** fluency studies of clinicians suggest grammatical errors matter less than comprehension errors. The highest-yield skill is often *understanding* the patient's tense choices, not producing perfect ones.

keyPoints: Motivo de consulta = chief complaint; enfermedad actual = present illness
Preterite marks completed, bounded events (empezó, me caí)
Imperfect paints background, ongoing states and habits (me dolía, estaba)
Interrupted-action frame: imperfect + cuando + preterite
Hace + time + que + present = still ongoing since then
Confirm the timeline with ¿Todavía lo tiene? and a summary back

test.explain: The motivo de consulta is the main reason the patient came in, the chief complaint.

test.q: How would a patient say "I fell yesterday" as a single completed event?
test.explain: A single completed action takes the preterite: me caí. Me caía is imperfect, which suggests a background or repeated action.

test.explain: Empezó marks the event (onset). Estaba haciendo is the imperfect progressive background.

test.q: Which phrase means "suddenly"?
test.explain: De repente means suddenly. Poco a poco means gradually.

test.q: "Hace tres días que me duele" means:
choices: The pain lasted three days last month
The pain comes three times each day
The pain began three days ago and continues
The pain will last about three days
test.explain: Hace + time + que + present describes something that started then and is still ongoing.

test.q: Which time phrase most strongly signals the imperfect?
test.explain: Todas las mañanas signals a habitual or repeated action, which takes the imperfect. The others point to specific, completed moments, which usually take the preterite.

test.q: "¿Se le corre a otra parte?" asks about the pain's:
test.explain: It asks whether the pain spreads elsewhere, which is radiation.

test.q: Formally asking "When did it start?": "¿Cuándo ___?"
test.explain: Onset is a single completed event, so it takes the preterite empezó (usted form).

test.q: What Spanish term (two words) means history of present illness?
test.explain: Enfermedad actual is standard; padecimiento actual is common in Mexico.

test.q: Del uno al ___, ¿qué tan fuerte es el dolor?
test.explain: The standard pain scale question uses a range of one to ten.

test.q: "I fainted" in Spanish: Me ___.
test.explain: Desmayarse in the preterite: me desmayé, a completed event.

advancedTest.q: A patient says "Estuve mareado toda la mañana." What does the preterite most likely imply?
choices: The dizziness is expected to start later
The dizziness was a bounded episode, now over
The dizziness is ongoing as they speak
advancedTest.explain: Perfective aspect presents the episode as a whole with an endpoint, implying it resolved. Confirm with ¿Todavía lo tiene?

advancedTest.q: A patient from Madrid says "Esta mañana he vomitado dos veces." How should you interpret it?
choices: Vomiting that is likely to happen later
A habit of vomiting each morning
Vomiting is still occurring right now
advancedTest.explain: In much of Spain, the present perfect marks completed events in the current time frame. It means the same as vomité in Latin America.

advancedTest.q: "Supe que tenía diabetes en 2019" best means:
choices: I found out I had diabetes in 2019
I used to have diabetes until 2019
I had long known about my diabetes
advancedTest.explain: Saber in the preterite shifts meaning to "found out"; tenía is the backshifted imperfect of reported content.

advancedTest.q: For a suspected thunderclap headache, which question best tests onset?
choices: ¿El dolor llegó a su máximo en segundos?
¿Qué lo mejora y qué lo empeora?
¿Le dolía la cabeza todos los días?
¿Se le corre el dolor a otra parte?
advancedTest.explain: Thunderclap headache peaks within seconds to about a minute. Patients use de repente loosely, so time to peak is the discriminating question.

lessons.title: Antecedentes personales: Past Medical and Surgical History

levels.kid:
When you meet a new doctor, they want to know your health story from before today. Did you ever break a bone? Did you ever sleep in a hospital? In Spanish, doctors call this story **antecedentes** (ahn-teh-seh-DEN-tes). It means "things that came before."

Here are some words a Spanish-speaking doctor might use:
- **¿Alguna vez...?** means "Have you ever...?"
- **operación** means operation, when a surgeon fixes something inside you.
- **hospital** is the same word in Spanish, but you say it "os-pee-TAL" with a quiet h.

So a doctor might ask: "¿Alguna vez tuvo una operación?" That means "Did you ever have an operation?" It is like a detective asking about old clues.
levels.hs:
After the chief complaint, a clinician asks about the patient's **antecedentes personales**, which are past medical and surgical history. These are illnesses, hospital stays and operations that happened before today's visit.

Key vocabulary:
- **enfermedades crónicas** (chronic illnesses) such as **diabetes**, **presión alta** (high blood pressure, formally *hipertensión*), **asma** and **epilepsia**
- **hospitalización** (hospital stay); *¿Lo/La han hospitalizado?* means "Have you been hospitalized?"
- **cirugía** or **operación** (surgery)
- **accidente** and **fractura** (accident, broken bone)

The most useful frame is **¿Alguna vez...?** ("Ever...?"):
- *¿Alguna vez ha tenido una cirugía?* Have you ever had surgery?
- *¿Tiene alguna enfermedad crónica?* Do you have any chronic illness?

The first question uses the **present perfect** (*ha tenido*, "have had"), made with *haber* plus a past participle. When the patient gives details, switch to the **preterite** for finished events: *¿Cuándo lo operaron?* (When did they operate on you?) The patient might answer *Me operaron de la vesícula en 2015* (I had gallbladder surgery in 2015).

Notice *me operaron*. Spanish speakers usually say "they operated on me" rather than "I had an operation." Learn this form, because you will hear it constantly.

A real example: a patient says *Tengo azúcar*. Literally this means "I have sugar," but it commonly means diabetes.
levels.college:
Taking the past medical history (PMH) and past surgical history (PSH) in Spanish depends on three grammar tools and a set of colloquial terms patients really use.

**1. Present perfect for screening.** *Haber* + participle asks about life experience up to now:
- *¿Ha estado hospitalizado/a alguna vez?*
- *¿Le han hecho alguna cirugía?* (Have they done any surgery on you?)
- *¿Le han dicho que tiene...?* (Have you been told you have...?) This is useful for diagnoses the patient may not name.

In much of Latin America the preterite is used even here (*¿Alguna vez tuvo una cirugía?*). Both are correct. Recognize both and use whichever your patient uses.

**2. Preterite for dated events.** *¿En qué año?* *¿Por qué lo operaron?* Use **hace + time** for "ago": *hace cinco años* (five years ago).

**3. Impersonal third-person plural.** *Me operaron de la rodilla*, *Me sacaron el apéndice* (they took out my appendix). The preposition **de** marks the organ: *operar de* + body part.

**Lay terms to recognize:**
- *azúcar alta* / *tengo azúcar*: diabetes
- *presión alta*: hypertension
- *ataques*, *convulsiones*: seizures
- *derrame* (*derrame cerebral*): stroke
- *ataque al corazón* / *infarto*: myocardial infarction
- *la tiroides*: thyroid disease

**Structured checklist:**
- Chronic illnesses (*diabetes, presión alta, enfermedades del corazón, pulmones, riñones*)
- Hospitalizations and the reason for each
- Surgeries, with year and complications (*¿Hubo complicaciones?*)
- Injuries (*golpes en la cabeza*, *fracturas*)
- For women: pregnancies (*¿Cuántos embarazos ha tenido?*)

Close with an open catch-all: *¿Hay algún otro problema de salud que debo saber?* (Is there any other health problem I should know about?)
levels.phd:
At graduate depth, eliciting PMH/PSH in Spanish is an exercise in **aspect, register and semantic mapping**.

**Aspect and dialect.** Peninsular Spanish uses the *pretérito perfecto* (*he tenido*) for experiential questions and for events within a time frame that is still current. Most Latin American varieties, including Mexican Spanish, the largest group in US clinics, prefer the *pretérito indefinido* (*tuve*) even for "ever" questions. A Mexican patient answering *¿Ha tenido cirugías?* with *Sí, tuve una* is aligning with dialect norms, not making an error. Experiential *alguna vez* works with either tense.

**Imperfect for chronic background.** The imperfect describes ongoing past states: *De niño tenía asma* (As a child I had asthma). The preterite marks a bounded episode: *Tuve una crisis de asma en 2019*. This contrast lets the clinician tell a chronic condition apart from a single event.

**Agentless plural.** *Me operaron*, *me internaron* (they admitted me), *me pusieron una placa* (they put in a plate) present the patient as experiencer, not agent. Asking *¿Qué le hicieron?* (What did they do to you?) often draws out procedures better than *¿Qué cirugía tuvo?*

**Semantic false friends and gaps:**
- *Derrame* can mean stroke, but *derrame* alone may also mean an effusion. *Derrame cerebral* versus *embolia* is often used loosely by patients.
- *Ataque* may mean seizure, panic attack or heart attack, so ask for clarification: *¿Qué pasó durante el ataque?*
- *Me operaron de la matriz* (womb) usually means hysterectomy, but confirm what was removed.
- *Anemia* and *colesterol* are generally understood. *Hipertensión* may be misread as nervous tension (*tensión nerviosa*).

**Diagnosis versus being told.** *¿Algún médico le ha dicho que tiene...?* moves the question from self-diagnosis to clinician-confirmed diagnosis. This matters because lay labels like *azúcar* or *nervios* do not map neatly onto biomedical categories. *Nervios* is a recognized cultural idiom of distress, not a diagnosis.
levels.expert:
For the clinician-scientist, the risk in Spanish PMH is not grammar but **false completeness**: a fluent-sounding history that silently drops data.

**Pitfalls in practice:**
- **Negative answers to category words.** *¿Tiene problemas del corazón?* may get *no* from a patient taking an antihypertensive, because they see *presión* as separate from *corazón*. Ask about specific named conditions and medicines (detailed medications belong to the next lesson).
- **Procedures not seen as surgery.** Cesareans (*cesárea*), tubal ligation (*operación para no tener hijos*, *ligadura*), cardiac catheterization and endoscopy are often left out. Ask *¿Le han hecho algún procedimiento, aunque no fuera una operación grande?*
- **Care received abroad.** Ask *¿Lo atendieron aquí o en su país?* Records may be unavailable, so get the institution, approximate year and any implants: *¿Tiene algún metal, placa, válvula o aparato en el cuerpo?* This matters directly for MRI safety.
- **Neurosurgical relevance.** Ask about prior head trauma (*¿Alguna vez se golpeó la cabeza y perdió el conocimiento?*), shunts (*válvula en la cabeza*), and previous spine surgery (*¿Lo han operado de la columna?*). Many Latin American patients with neurocysticercosis say *tuve gusanos/quistes en el cerebro* or *ataques desde joven*. Treat this as a serious lead, not vague history.

**Interpreter-aware phrasing.** Avoid stacked questions (*¿Ha tenido diabetes, presión alta o asma?*). They invite a single *no*. One condition per question gives cleaner yes/no answers and helps interpreters.

**Evidence and equity.** Studies of ad hoc interpreters and partly fluent clinicians show clinically significant errors, especially omissions. Joint Commission and Title VI expectations push toward qualified interpreters unless the clinician's proficiency has been formally assessed. Use your Spanish to build rapport and screen, and confirm critical history with a professional interpreter.

**Grammar refinement for natural speech:** use *usted* forms consistently and *operado/operada* by patient gender. *¿Desde cuándo tiene diabetes?* (since when) pairs naturally with the present tense, unlike the English "have had," a common error among anglophone learners.

keyPoints: Antecedentes personales = past medical and surgical history
¿Alguna vez...? frames 'have you ever' questions
Present perfect (ha tenido) to screen; preterite for dated events
Patients say 'me operaron de...' (they operated on me for...)
Know lay terms: azúcar = diabetes, presión alta, derrame, ataques
Ask about implants, procedures and care abroad to avoid gaps

lessons.title: Medicamentos y alergias: Asking About Medicines and Allergies

levels.kid:
When you visit a doctor, they want to know two big things. What medicines do you take? And is anything bad for your body?

In Spanish, medicine is **medicina** or **medicamento**. A doctor might ask: **¿Toma medicinas?** That means "Do you take medicines?"

An **alergia** is when your body acts like a guard dog barking at something harmless, like peanuts or bee stings. Your skin might get itchy bumps, or your face might swell.

So the doctor asks: **¿Tiene alergias?** That means "Do you have allergies?"

These questions keep you safe. The doctor never wants to give you a medicine your body does not like. Knowing the words in Spanish helps doctors protect many more kids.
levels.hs:
Asking about **medicamentos** (medications) and **alergias** (allergies) is one of the most important safety steps in any interview. A wrong answer here can lead to a dangerous drug reaction.

Key questions (formal **usted** form):
- **¿Toma algún medicamento?** Do you take any medication?
- **¿Toma vitaminas, hierbas o remedios caseros?** Do you take vitamins, herbs or home remedies?
- **¿Es alérgico/alérgica a algún medicamento?** Are you allergic to any medication?
- **¿Qué le pasó?** What happened to you? (to describe the reaction)

Useful vocabulary:
- **la pastilla / la tableta**: pill / tablet
- **el jarabe**: syrup
- **la inyección**: injection
- **la receta**: prescription
- **sin receta**: over the counter (literally "without prescription")
- **las ronchas / la urticaria**: hives

A real example: a patient says, **"Soy alérgica a la penicilina. Me salieron ronchas."** ("I'm allergic to penicillin. I broke out in hives.") Notice **salieron** is preterite, a finished event in the past.

Watch out for a famous false friend: **intoxicado/a** usually means "poisoned" or sick from something ingested, not "drunk." Also, **constipado** often means having a cold, not constipation. Always confirm unclear words.
levels.college:
A complete medication history in Spanish covers prescription drugs, over-the-counter products, supplements, traditional remedies, and adherence. The allergy history then separates true allergy from side effects.

**Medication questions**
- **¿Qué medicamentos toma actualmente?** What medications do you currently take?
- **¿Para qué lo toma?** What do you take it for?
- **¿Cuántas veces al día lo toma?** How many times a day do you take it? (frequency only; confirm details from the bottle)
- **¿Me puede mostrar los frascos?** Can you show me the bottles?
- **¿Se le olvida tomarlo a veces?** Do you sometimes forget to take it?
- **¿Usa algún té, hierba o remedio casero?** Do you use any tea, herb or home remedy?

Note the pronoun **lo** (it, masculine, for *el medicamento*) or **la** (for *la pastilla*). Asking for bottles is a strong habit: brand names differ between countries, so a patient's drug from Mexico may have an unfamiliar name.

**Allergy questions**
- **¿Es alérgico a algún medicamento, alimento o al látex?** Allergic to any medication, food, or latex?
- **¿Qué reacción tuvo?** What reaction did you have?
- **¿Se le hinchó la cara o la garganta?** Did your face or throat swell?
- **¿Le costó respirar?** Was it hard to breathe?

**Tense matters.** Use the preterite for the single reaction (**me dio** ronchas, **se me hinchó** la boca) and the imperfect for background (**tenía** diez años, **estaba** en el hospital).

**Allergy vs. side effect.** Nausea after a pill (**me dio náusea**) is usually an intolerance or side effect (**efecto secundario**), not an allergy. Hives, swelling, wheezing or fainting suggest a true allergic reaction. Clarifying this prevents patients from being labeled allergic unnecessarily.
levels.phd:
Grammatically, the medication and allergy history showcases Spanish **pronominal and dative constructions** that English speakers often mishandle.

**Reactions with gustar-type verbs.** Spanish frames reactions with the body part as subject and the patient as indirect object: **Me salieron ronchas** (hives came out on me), **Se me hinchó la lengua** (my tongue swelled on me). The "se + indirect object" structure (**se me**, **se le**) marks an unplanned event happening to someone. Learners who say *"Yo hinché mi lengua"* produce something odd and agentive. Note the definite article with body parts (**la lengua**, not *mi lengua*), since the dative pronoun already shows possession.

**Agreement.** **Alérgico/alérgica** agrees with the patient's gender; **ser** is used for a lasting trait (**Soy alérgico**), while **tener** pairs with the noun (**Tengo alergia a**). The preposition is **a**: alérgico **a** la penicilina, never *de*.

**Lexical nuance.** **Remedio** can mean medicine or home remedy; **droga** in many regions implies illicit drugs, so clinical speakers prefer **medicamento**. **Pomada / crema** (ointment / cream), **gotas** (drops), **parche** (patch) and **inhalador** cover formulations.

**Clinical-linguistic accuracy.** Research on medical interpreting (e.g., Flores and colleagues' 2003 *Pediatrics* study of interpreter errors) found that errors of omission were most common, and that ad hoc interpreters, such as family members, made errors with potential clinical consequences more often than trained interpreters. Allergy and medication information was among the content at risk. This is why clinicians with limited proficiency should use professional interpreters for high-stakes details and verify allergies with written lists.

**Cross-border pharmacology.** Patients may use products obtained abroad, sometimes sold without prescription, including antibiotics or injectables. Asking **¿Compró algún medicamento en otro país?** surfaces these. Traditional herbal products (e.g., **ruda**, **gordolobo**, **manzanilla**) may interact with prescribed drugs; nonjudgmental phrasing encourages disclosure.
levels.expert:
At the bedside, aim for precise, verifiable data rather than fluent-sounding conversation. A practical sequence uses **teach-back** and **closed confirmation**.

**Medication reconciliation phrasing**
- **Vamos a revisar sus medicamentos uno por uno.** Let's go through your medications one by one.
- **Dígame el nombre que dice la etiqueta.** Tell me the name on the label.
- **¿Alguien más le receta medicinas?** Does anyone else prescribe you medicines?
- **¿Dejó de tomar alguno recientemente? ¿Por qué?** Did you stop any recently? Why?

That last question catches abrupt discontinuation, highly relevant in neurosurgery: anticoagulants (**anticoagulantes**, "blood thinners": **¿Toma algo para adelgazar la sangre?**), antiplatelets such as **aspirina**, and antiepileptics (**medicamentos para las convulsiones**). Patients often say **"la pastilla para la presión"** or **"la del azúcar"** rather than drug names, so map indications to drugs and confirm with the pharmacy record.

**Allergy characterization in Spanish**
Document agent, reaction, timing and severity:
- **¿Cuánto tiempo después le pasó?** How long after did it happen?
- **¿Necesitó ir a emergencias?** Did you need the emergency room?
- **¿Ha vuelto a tomar ese medicamento u otro parecido?** Have you taken it or a similar one since?

The last question matters because most patients labeled penicillin-allergic are not truly allergic on formal evaluation, and the label drives use of broader-spectrum or less effective alternatives. Precise Spanish questioning supports later **de-labeling** by allergy services.

**Pitfalls**
- **Dosis by number**: Spanish numbers and units (miligramos vs. microgramos) are high-error zones; read labels rather than rely on recall.
- **Register**: rural or older patients may say **"me cayó mal"** (it disagreed with me), which can mean anything from nausea to anaphylaxis. Probe.
- **Contrast agent and latex**: ask explicitly before imaging or surgery: **¿Ha tenido reacción al medio de contraste o al látex?**

Open question for the field: structured bilingual allergy templates in electronic records remain inconsistent, and standards for documenting reactions reported in Spanish are still evolving.

lessons.title: Antecedentes familiares: Family Members and Inherited Conditions

levels.kid:
Doctors like to ask about your family. Why? Because some health problems can run in families, a bit like curly hair or brown eyes.

In Spanish, family words are fun:
- **mamá** or **madre** = mom
- **papá** or **padre** = dad
- **hermano** = brother, **hermana** = sister
- **abuelo** = grandpa, **abuela** = grandma

A Spanish-speaking doctor might ask: **¿Alguien en su familia tiene diabetes?** That means "Does anyone in your family have diabetes?"

If Grandma has a sick heart, the doctor will check your heart extra carefully. Knowing your family is like having a treasure map. It shows the doctor where to look first.
levels.hs:
**Antecedentes familiares** means "family history." It is the part of the interview where you ask which illnesses run in the patient's family, because many conditions, such as heart disease, diabetes and some cancers, are partly **hereditario** (hereditary).

Key family words:
- **padre / madre** (father / mother), **padres** (parents; careful, it does not mean "relatives")
- **hermano / hermana** (brother / sister)
- **hijo / hija** (son / daughter)
- **abuelo / abuela** (grandfather / grandmother)
- **tío / tía** (uncle / aunt), **primo / prima** (cousin)
- **pariente** or **familiar** (relative)

Useful questions:
- **¿Sus padres viven?** Are your parents living?
- **¿De qué murió su padre?** What did your father die of?
- **¿A qué edad?** At what age?
- **¿Hay alguien en su familia con presión alta, diabetes o cáncer?** Is there anyone in your family with high blood pressure, diabetes or cancer?

Notice the past tense: **murió** (died) is preterite because death is a completed event. Age matters a lot. A father who had a heart attack (**un infarto**) at 45 is a much bigger warning sign than one at 85.

Example: a doctor learns that a teenager's mother and grandmother both had breast cancer (**cáncer de mama**) young. That pattern can lead to genetic counseling.
levels.college:
The family history (**historia familiar** or **antecedentes heredofamiliares**, the latter common in Mexico) screens for conditions with a genetic or shared-environment component. Be systematic: go relative by relative, recording whether each is living, current conditions, and age at onset or death.

**Kinship vocabulary beyond the nuclear family:**
- **medio hermano / media hermana**: half-brother / half-sister
- **sobrino/a**: nephew/niece; **nieto/a**: grandchild
- **por parte de mi madre / del lado materno**: on my mother's side; **paterno**: paternal
- **gemelo/a**: twin; **gemelos idénticos** for identical twins

**Conditions to ask about by name** (patients may not recognize categories like "cardiovascular"):
- **presión alta / hipertensión**, **azúcar alta / diabetes**, **colesterol alto**
- **infarto (ataque al corazón)**, **derrame cerebral** or **embolia** (stroke, colloquial)
- **cáncer de colon, de mama, de ovario, de próstata**
- **convulsiones / epilepsia**, **aneurisma**, **demencia / Alzheimer**
- **muerte súbita** (sudden death), especially at a young age

**Grammar in the interview:**
- Preterite for completed events: **Mi abuelo murió de un derrame a los 60 años.**
- Imperfect for ongoing past states: **Mi madre tenía diabetes.**
- **Padecer de** (to suffer from) is common: **¿Alguien padece del corazón?** Does anyone have heart trouble?
- The phrase **a los ... años** gives age at an event: **a los 50 años** (at age 50).

Pitfalls: **pariente** means relative, not parent. **Embolia** in everyday speech often means stroke, not a pulmonary embolism, so clarify. Adoption matters: **¿Es usted adoptado/a?** tells you whether the biological history is known.
levels.phd:
Structured family history functions as a low-cost genomic screen, and in Spanish its quality depends on precise kinship mapping and age data. The standard output is a three-generation **árbol genealógico** (pedigree), and patients rarely volunteer the details that set inheritance patterns apart. Elicit them deliberately:

- **Laterality and lineage:** **¿Por parte de su madre o de su padre?** Two maternal relatives with early colorectal cancer suggest a different risk than one on each side.
- **Age at onset:** **¿Qué edad tenía cuando se lo diagnosticaron?** (How old was he/she when it was diagnosed?) Note the clitic pair **se lo** (indirect-object se, replacing le, plus direct-object lo).
- **Consanguinity:** **¿Sus padres son parientes entre sí, por ejemplo primos?** This is relevant to autosomal recessive conditions. Ask it neutrally.
- **Ancestry:** **¿De qué país o región es su familia?**

Neurologically relevant family items include **aneurismas cerebrales**. Intracranial aneurysm risk is notably higher with two or more affected first-degree relatives and with **poliquistosis renal autosómica dominante**. Others are **epilepsia**, **enfermedad de Huntington**, **esclerosis múltiple** and **neurofibromatosis (manchas café con leche)**. Lay patients may say **"se le reventó una vena en la cabeza"** (a vein burst in his head) for hemorrhagic stroke or a ruptured aneurysm.

Grammatical nuance: aspect encodes clinical meaning. **Murió de cáncer** (preterite) marks the event. **Sufría de convulsiones** (imperfect) marks a chronic background state. **Le dio un infarto** ("a heart attack came to him") is a very common dative construction worth recognizing.

Regional variation matters. **Antecedentes heredofamiliares (AHF)** is Mexican charting convention. **Azúcar** for diabetes and **la presión** for hypertension are widespread, and **derrame** and **embolia** vary by country in exactly what they mean. Studies of language-discordant care show that family histories taken through ad hoc interpreters are often incomplete, which supports professional interpretation or verified proficiency.
levels.expert:
Clinically, the family history in Spanish should produce actionable risk categories, not a list. Several practical refinements help.

**Fluent elicitation phrasing:**
- **Voy a preguntarle por la salud de su familia de sangre.** I'm going to ask about the health of your blood relatives. This excludes in-laws (**suegros, cuñados**) and step-relatives (**padrastro, madrastra, hermanastro**), which patients often include.
- **¿Alguien en la familia falleció joven, antes de los 50, sin saberse por qué?** This screens for unexplained early death.
- **¿Alguien se ha hecho un estudio genético?** Has anyone had genetic testing? Ask for the report. A documented variant in a relative changes the workup.

**Register and sensitivity:** **Fallecer** is gentler than **morir** when asking about deaths. Use **usted** throughout. Some families know a diagnosis only as **"algo de la sangre"** or **"un tumor"**. Probe with **¿Le operaron? ¿Le dieron quimioterapia?** to infer the type. Mistaken paternity, adoption and family estrangement can make data unknowable. Document **"desconocido"** rather than "negative."

**Grammar notes:** In **se lo diagnosticaron a los 40**, the impersonal third-person plural avoids naming who diagnosed it. **Tenía** versus **tuvo** carries meaning: **tuvo un derrame** is a discrete event, while **tenía la presión alta** is a chronic state. **Ninguno** (nobody) agrees in gender: **ninguna de mis hermanas**.

**Neurosurgical relevance:** For a patient with a newly found unruptured aneurysm, ask **¿Algún familiar tuvo un aneurisma o una hemorragia en el cerebro?** Two or more affected first-degree relatives define familial intracranial aneurysm and support screening first-degree relatives. In a child with a spinal cord tumor or multiple **manchas café con leche**, the family history guides evaluation for NF1 or NF2-related schwannomatosis.

**Open issues:** Patient-completed digital family-history tools exist in Spanish, but cultural concepts of kinship and limited health literacy still require clinician verification. Underuse of family history in Spanish-speaking populations contributes to inequities in referral for genetic counseling.

keyPoints: Antecedentes familiares means family history
Core words: padre, madre, hermano, abuelo, tío, primo, hijo
Pariente means relative, not parent
Ask age at onset or death: ¿A qué edad?
Preterite for events (murió), imperfect for chronic states (tenía)
Clarify lay terms like derrame and embolia, and maternal vs paternal side

lessons.title: Hábitos y vida diaria: Work, Diet, Exercise, Tobacco and Alcohol

levels.kid:
Doctors want to know about your whole day, not just where it hurts. What you eat, how you play, and how you sleep all help keep your body healthy.

Here are some Spanish words a doctor might use:
- **trabajo** = work
- **comida** = food
- **ejercicio** = exercise
- **dormir** = to sleep
- **fumar** = to smoke

A doctor might ask a grown-up, "¿Hace ejercicio?" That means "Do you exercise?" Or "¿Fuma?" That means "Do you smoke?"

These are like clues in a detective game. Smoking can hurt the lungs and heart. Moving your body makes your heart strong. When the doctor knows your habits, the doctor can give you better advice to stay healthy.
levels.hs:
Every medical interview includes the **social history**, which is information about a patient's daily life. In Spanish clinics it is often called **hábitos** or **historia social**. It covers work, diet, exercise, sleep, tobacco and alcohol, because these habits raise or lower the risk of many diseases.

Useful questions (using the polite **usted** form):
- **¿A qué se dedica?** What do you do for work?
- **¿Qué come en un día normal?** What do you eat on a normal day?
- **¿Hace ejercicio? ¿Con qué frecuencia?** Do you exercise? How often?
- **¿Cuántas horas duerme?** How many hours do you sleep?
- **¿Fuma?** Do you smoke? **¿Ha fumado alguna vez?** Have you ever smoked?
- **¿Toma bebidas alcohólicas?** Do you drink alcoholic beverages?

Notice that **tomar** means "to take" but also "to drink." In many Latin American countries, "¿Usted toma?" by itself means "Do you drink alcohol?"

Answers about habits use the **present tense**: "Camino todos los días" (I walk every day). Frequency words help: **todos los días** (every day), **a veces** (sometimes), **de vez en cuando** (once in a while), **nunca** (never).

Example: a construction worker says, "Trabajo en construcción y fumo diez cigarrillos al día." That tells the doctor about possible dust exposure and lung risk.
levels.college:
The social history (**hábitos**, **historia social**, or in Mexico **antecedentes personales no patológicos**) needs both good questions and accurate quantification.

**Work (trabajo)**
- ¿En qué trabaja? / ¿A qué se dedica?
- ¿Trabaja con químicos, polvo, ruido o plaguicidas? (chemicals, dust, noise, pesticides)
- ¿Levanta cosas pesadas? (Do you lift heavy things?), which matters for back pain.

**Diet and activity (dieta y actividad)**
- ¿Cuántas comidas hace al día? How many meals a day?
- ¿Come frutas y verduras? ¿Toma refrescos? (sodas)
- ¿Cuántas veces por semana hace ejercicio? ¿Por cuánto tiempo?

**Tobacco (tabaco)**
- ¿Fuma cigarrillos? ¿Vapea o usa cigarrillo electrónico?
- ¿Cuántos cigarrillos al día? ¿Desde qué edad?
- If they quit: **¿Hace cuánto tiempo dejó de fumar?** How long ago did you quit?
- Clinicians calculate **paquetes-año** (pack-years); Mexico also uses **índice tabáquico**.

**Alcohol**
- ¿Toma alcohol? ¿Qué toma: cerveza, vino, licor?
- ¿Cuántas bebidas toma en una semana normal?

**Key grammar**
- Present for current habits: *Fumo*, *Camino*.
- **Soler + infinitive** for "usually": *Suelo caminar por la mañana* (I usually walk in the morning).
- **Imperfect** for past habits: *Fumaba un paquete al día* (I used to smoke a pack a day).
- **Preterite** for a completed change: *Dejé de fumar en 2019* (I quit smoking in 2019).
- **Dejar de + infinitive** = to stop doing: *dejar de tomar*.

**Regional words:** in Mexico **cigarro** usually means a cigarette, while elsewhere it can mean a cigar. A hangover is **cruda** in Mexico and **resaca** in Spain.
levels.phd:
Social history in Spanish depends on tense and aspect, because the main clinical question is when a habit started, how long it lasted, and whether it continues.

**Duration constructions**
- **Hace + time + que + present**: *Hace veinte años que fumo* = I have smoked for twenty years and still do.
- **Llevar + time + gerund**: *Llevo veinte años fumando*, which has the same meaning and is very common in speech.
- **Hace + time + preterite**: *Dejé de fumar hace cinco años* = I quit five years ago.
- **Desde hace**: *No tomo desde hace un año* = I haven't drunk for a year.

The first two describe ongoing exposure, and the last two describe cessation. Mixing them up can turn a current smoker into a former smoker in the record.

**Aspect contrast**
- Imperfect *fumaba*, *tomaba* = habitual past, with no endpoint stated.
- Preterite *fumé durante diez años* = a bounded period that is now finished.
- The perfect *¿Ha fumado alguna vez?* asks about lifetime ever-use, the standard first screening question.

**Quantification**
- Pack-years = packs per day × years smoked. *Un paquete al día durante treinta años* gives 30 paquetes-año.
- For alcohol, use frequency and quantity questions: *¿Con qué frecuencia toma? ¿Cuántas bebidas en un día típico? ¿Con qué frecuencia toma seis o más?* These follow the **AUDIT-C**, which has validated Spanish versions.

**Validated Spanish CAGE items**
- ¿Ha sentido que debería beber menos?
- ¿Le ha molestado que la gente critique su forma de beber?
- ¿Se ha sentido culpable por beber?
- ¿Ha bebido por la mañana para calmar los nervios o quitarse la cruda? (the "eye-opener")

**Lexical ambiguity**
- *Tomar* alone suggests alcohol in much of Latin America.
- A *copa* or *trago* is a vague unit, and *una caguama* (Mexico) is a large beer bottle. Ask what size the drink is.

**Nuance:** *Bebo socialmente* (I drink socially) contains no number. Follow up with *¿Cuántas bebidas en una semana normal?*
levels.expert:
In practice the language problem is less about vocabulary and more about underreporting, framing and documentation.

**Normalizing questions** reduce stigma. Compare *¿Toma alcohol?*, which invites "no," with *Muchas personas toman algo de alcohol. En una semana normal, ¿cuántas cervezas toma usted?*. Asking "how many" assumes the behavior is possible and generally gives more accurate numbers. Pair it with a reason: *Le pregunto porque afecta la anestesia y la cicatrización* (it affects anesthesia and healing).

**Neurosurgical relevance**
- Smoking is a major modifiable risk factor for intracranial aneurysm growth and rupture. *¿Sigue fumando?* matters for counseling.
- Nicotine impairs bone fusion. Smokers have higher rates of nonunion (**pseudoartrosis**) after spinal fusion, so ask about vaping and nicotine replacement too: *¿Usa parches, chicles o vapeador?*
- Heavy alcohol use is linked to falls, chronic subdural hematoma and perioperative withdrawal (**síndrome de abstinencia**). Ask *¿Cuándo fue su última bebida?* to plan monitoring.
- Occupation shapes recovery: *¿Su trabajo requiere cargar peso o manejar?* (lifting, driving) helps plan return-to-work after spine or head surgery.

**Pitfalls**
- *Cigarro* means a cigarette to Mexican patients, but a Spaniard may hear "cigar."
- *Ex fumador* covers anyone from yesterday's quitter to someone who quit decades ago, so document the date.
- *Una copa* in Spain and *un trago* in the Caribbean vary hugely in volume.
- *Hago ejercicio* may mean demanding farm labor (*trabajo en el campo*). Ask for minutes and intensity.
- Food words vary by region (*tortillas, arepas, pan dulce*). Ask about *refrescos* and *jugos* separately, because patients may not count them as sugar.

**Documentation in Spanish-language records**: *Tabaquismo positivo, índice tabáquico 15 paquetes-año; alcoholismo negado* (alcohol use denied). In Mexican charts **alcoholismo** often just means "alcohol use" as a heading, not a diagnosis. Don't translate it literally into an English note.

**Open question:** most Spanish screening tools were validated in Spain or Mexico, so how well they perform across other dialects and in US bilingual settings is still under study.

keyPoints: Social history = hábitos: work, diet, exercise, sleep, tobacco, alcohol
¿A qué se dedica? asks about work; ask about exposures (químicos, polvo)
Tomar can mean 'to drink alcohol'; quantify drinks per week
Present tense and soler for current habits; imperfect for past habits
Dejé de fumar hace + time = quit ago; llevo + time + gerund = still ongoing
Pack-years = paquetes-año; normalize questions to reduce underreporting

test.q: What does "¿A qué se dedica?" ask a patient?
choices: What do you do for work?
test.explain: ¿A qué se dedica? is the standard polite way to ask about someone's occupation.

test.q: In "¿Toma bebidas alcohólicas?", the verb tomar means:
test.explain: Tomar means 'to take' but is the everyday verb for drinking. In much of Latin America it implies alcohol even when used alone.

test.q: "¿Con qué frecuencia hace ejercicio?" asks the patient:
test.explain: Con qué frecuencia means 'how often.' Duration would be ¿Por cuánto tiempo?

test.q: A patient says "Fumaba." The imperfect tense suggests:
test.explain: The imperfect describes a habitual past action. A single event would use the preterite (fumé).

test.q: "Dejé de fumar hace cinco años" means:
choices: I will quit within five years
I quit smoking five years ago
I have smoked for five years
test.explain: Dejar de + infinitive means 'to stop doing,' and hace + time with the preterite means 'ago.'

test.q: What is the Spanish clinical term for pack-years?
test.explain: Paquetes-año (packs per day × years). Mexico also uses índice tabáquico.

test.q: Which question screens for workplace exposures?
test.explain: It asks whether the patient works with chemicals or dust, a classic occupational exposure question.

test.q: To a Mexican patient, the word "cigarro" usually means:
test.explain: In Mexico cigarro usually means a cigarette. In other regions it can mean a cigar, so clarify.

test.q: Why should a clinician follow up on "Bebo socialmente"?
choices: It gives no number of drinks
It is rude to say in Spanish
test.explain: 'I drink socially' is vague. Ask ¿Cuántas bebidas en una semana normal? to quantify.

test.q: What is the Spanish verb meaning 'to smoke'?
test.explain: Fumar: ¿Fuma? = Do you smoke?

test.q: ___ caminar por la mañana. (I usually walk in the morning.)
test.explain: Soler + infinitive expresses a usual habit. Suelo is the first-person present form.

test.q: ¿Cuántas horas ___ por la noche? (How many hours do you sleep at night?)
test.explain: Duerme is the usted form of dormir (o→ue stem change).

kidTest.explain: Fumar means to smoke. Smoking can hurt the lungs and heart.
Ejercicio means exercise, which makes your heart strong.

kidTest.q: Why does a doctor ask about your habits?
kidTest.explain: Habits are clues that help the doctor keep you healthy.
Comida means food.

kidTest.q: What is the Spanish word for work? (t _ _ _ _ _ _)
kidTest.explain: Trabajo means work.

advancedTest.q: A patient says "Llevo veinte años fumando." How should this be documented?
choices: Smoked once, twenty years in the past
Former smoker who quit twenty years ago
Plans to begin smoking within the year
Current smoker with twenty years of use
advancedTest.explain: Llevar + time + gerund describes an ongoing action. Quitting would be phrased Dejé de fumar hace veinte años.

advancedTest.q: Which Spanish CAGE item corresponds to the 'eye-opener' question?
choices: ¿Ha bebido por la mañana para la cruda?
advancedTest.explain: The eye-opener asks about morning drinking to calm nerves or relieve a hangover, which suggests dependence.

advancedTest.q: Before spinal fusion, why ask about vaping and nicotine patches, not just cigarettes?
advancedTest.explain: Nicotine from any source impairs bone fusion and raises the risk of nonunion (pseudoartrosis). Asking only about cigarettes would miss these sources.

advancedTest.q: Why ask "¿Cuántas cervezas toma en una semana normal?" rather than "¿Toma alcohol?"
choices: It refers to tobacco and alcohol together
It avoids using the usted form
It presumes use and reduces underreporting
advancedTest.explain: A normalizing 'how many' question makes disclosure easier and gives a number. A yes/no question invites a quick denial.
